u1s1: A belt is a loop of flexible material used to link two or more rotating shafts mechanically, most often parallel.
u2s1: Belts may be used as a source of motion, to transmit power efficiently or to track relative movement.
u3s1: Belts are looped over pulleys and may have a twist between the pulleys, and the shafts need not be parallel.
u4s1: In a two pulley system, the belt can either drive the pulleys normally in one direction (the same if on parallel shafts), or the belt may be crossed, so that the direction of the driven shaft is reversed (the opposite direction to the driver if on parallel shafts).
u5s1: The belt drive can also be used to change the speed of rotation, either up or down, by using different sized pulleys.
u6s1: As a source of motion, a conveyor belt is one application where the belt is adapted to carry a load continuously between two points.
u7s1: == History == The mechanical belt drive, using a pulley machine, was first mentioned in the text of the Dictionary of Local Expressions by the Han Dynasty philosopher, poet, and politician Yang Xiong (53–18 BC) in 15 BC, used for a quilling machine that wound silk fibres onto bobbins for weavers' shuttles.
u8s1: The belt drive is an essential component of the invention of the spinning wheel.
u9s1: The belt drive was not only used in textile technologies, it was also applied to hydraulic-powered bellows dated from the 1st century AD.
u10s1: == Power transmission == Belts are the cheapest utility for power transmission between shafts that may not be axially aligned.
u11s1: Power transmission is achieved by purposely designed belts and pulleys.
u12s1: The variety of power transmission needs that can be met by a belt-drive transmission system are numerous, and this has led to many variations on the theme.
u13s1: A drawback to belt drives is that they transmit less power than gears or chain drives.
u14s1: However, improvements in belt engineering allow use of belts in systems that formerly only allowed chain drives or gears.
u15s1: Power transmitted between a belt and a pulley is expressed as the product of difference of tension and belt velocity:
u16s1: v , {\displaystyle P=(T_{1}-T_{2})v,} where T 1 {\displaystyle T_{1}} and T 2 {\displaystyle T_{2}} are tensions in the tight side and slack side of the belt respectively.
u17s1: Clutch action can be achieved by shifting the belt to a free turning pulley or by releasing belt tension.
u18s1: However, this problem can be largely solved by the use of toothed belts.
u19s1: === Flat belts === Flat belts were widely used in the 19th and early 20th centuries in line shafting to transmit power in factories.
u20s1: Flat belts are still used today, although not nearly as much as in the line-shaft era.
u21s1: The flat belt is a simple system of power transmission that was well suited for its day.
u22s1: It can deliver high power at high speeds (373 kW at 51 m/s; 115 mph), in cases of wide belts and large pulleys.
u23s1: Wide-belt-large-pulley drives are bulky, consuming much space while requiring high tension, leading to high loads, and are poorly suited to close-centers applications.
u24s1: V-belts have mainly replaced flat belts for short-distance power transmission; and longer-distance power transmission is typically no longer done with belts at all.
u25s1: Because flat belts tend to climb towards the higher side of the pulley, pulleys were made with a slightly convex or "crowned" surface (rather than flat) to allow the belt to self-center as it runs.
u26s1: Flat belts also tend to slip on the pulley face when heavy loads are applied, and many proprietary belt dressings were available that could be applied to the belts to increase friction, and so power transmission.
u27s1: Flat belts were traditionally made of leather or fabric.
u28s1: Early flour mills in Ukraine had leather belt drives.
u29s1: After World War I, there was such a shortage of shoe leather that people cut up the belt drives to make shoes.
u30s1: Leather drive belts were put to another use during the Rhodesian Bush War (1964–1979): To protect riders of cars and busses from land mines, layers of leather belt drives were placed on the floors of vehicles in danger zones.
u31s1: Today most belt drives are made of rubber or synthetic polymers.
u32s1: Grip of leather belts is often better if they are assembled with the hair side (outer side) of the leather against the pulley, although some belts are instead given a half-twist before joining the ends (forming a Möbius strip), so that wear can be evenly distributed on both sides of the belt.
u33s1: Belts ends are joined by lacing the ends together with leather thonging (the oldest of the methods), steel comb fasteners and/or lacing, or by gluing or welding (in the case of polyurethane or polyester).
u34s1: Flat belts were traditionally jointed, and still usually are, but they can also be made with endless construction.
u35s1: === Rope drives === In the mid 19th century, British millwrights discovered that multi-grooved pulleys connected by ropes outperformed flat pulleys connected by leather belts.
u36s1: In general, as with flat belts, rope drives were used for connections from stationary engines to the jack shafts and line shafts of mills, and sometimes from line shafts to driven machinery.
u37s1: Unlike leather belts, however, rope drives were sometimes used to transmit power over relatively long distances.
u38s1: === Round belts === Round belts are a circular cross section belt designed to run in a pulley with a 60 degree V-groove.
u39s1: Round grooves are only suitable for idler pulleys that guide the belt, or when (soft) O-ring type belts are used.
u40s1: Nevertheless, round belts are for use in relatively low torque situations only and may be purchased in various lengths or cut to length and joined, either by a staple, a metallic connector (in the case of hollow plastic), gluing or welding (in the case of polyurethane).
u41s1: Early sewing machines utilized a leather belt, joined either by a metal staple or glued, to great effect.
u42s1: === Spring belts === Spring belts are similar to rope or round belts but consist of a long steel helical spring.
u43s1: The main advantage over rubber or other elastic belts is that they last much longer under poorly controlled operating conditions.
u44s1: The ends of a spring belt can be joined either by bending the last turn of the helix at each end by 90 degrees to form hooks, or by reducing the diameter of the last few turns at one end so that it "screws" into the other end.
u45s1: === V belts === V belts (also style V-belts, vee belts, or, less commonly, wedge rope) solved the slippage and alignment problem.
u46s1: It is now the basic belt for power transmission.
u47s1: The "V" shape of the belt tracks in a mating groove in the pulley (or sheave), with the result that the belt cannot slip off.
u48s1: The belt also tends to wedge into the groove as the load increases—the greater the load, the greater the wedging action—improving torque transmission and making the V-belt an effective solution, needing less width and tension than flat belts.
u49s1: V-belts trump flat belts with their small center distances and high reduction ratios.
u50s1: V-belts need larger pulleys for their thicker cross-section than flat belts.
u51s1: For high-power requirements, two or more V-belts can be joined side-by-side in an arrangement called a multi-V, running on matching multi-groove sheaves.
u52s1: This is known as a multiple-V-belt drive (or sometimes a "classical V-belt drive").
u53s1: V-belts may be homogeneously rubber or polymer throughout, or there may be fibers embedded in the rubber or polymer for strength and reinforcement.
u54s1: When an endless belt does not fit the need, jointed and link V-belts may be employed.
u55s1: Most models offer the same power and speed ratings as equivalently-sized endless belts and do not require special pulleys to operate.
u56s1: A link v-belt is a number of polyurethane/polyester composite links held together, either by themselves, such as Fenner Drives' PowerTwist, or Nu-T-Link (with metal studs).
u57s1: These provide easy installation and superior environmental resistance compared to rubber belts and are length-adjustable by disassembling and removing links when needed.
u58s1: ==== History of V-belts ==== Trade journal coverage of V-belts in automobiles from 1916 mentioned leather as the belt material, and mentioned that the V angle was not yet well standardized.
u59s1: The endless rubber V-belt was developed in 1917 by Charles C. Gates of the Gates Rubber Company.
u60s1: Multiple-V-belt drive was first arranged a few years later by Walter Geist of the Allis-Chalmers corporation, who was inspired to replace the single rope of multi-groove-sheave rope drives with multiple V-belts running parallel.
u61s1: The "Texrope" brand still exists, although it has changed ownership and no longer refers to multiple-V-belt drive alone.
u62s1: === Multi-groove belts === A multi-groove, V-ribbed, or polygroove belt is made up of usually between 3 and 24 V-shaped sections alongside each other.
u63s1: This gives a thinner belt for the same drive surface, thus it is more flexible, although often wider.
u64s1: The added flexibility offers an improved efficiency, as less energy is wasted in the internal friction of continually bending the belt.
u65s1: In practice this gain of efficiency causes a reduced heating effect on the belt, and a cooler-running belt lasts longer in service.
u66s1: Belts are commercially available in several sizes, with usually a 'P' (sometimes omitted) and a single letter identifying the pitch between grooves.
u67s1: A further advantage of the polygroove belt that makes them popular is that they can run over pulleys on the ungrooved back of the belt.
u68s1: Though this is sometimes done with V-belts with a single idler pulley for tensioning, a polygroove belt may be wrapped around a pulley on its back tightly enough to change its direction, or even to provide a light driving force.
u69s1: Any V-belt's ability to drive pulleys depends on wrapping the belt around a sufficient angle of the pulley to provide grip.
u70s1: Where a single-V-belt is limited to a simple convex shape, it can adequately wrap at most three or possibly four pulleys, so can drive at most three accessories.
u71s1: Where more must be driven, such as for modern cars with power steering and air conditioning, multiple belts are required.
u72s1: As the polygroove belt can be bent into concave paths by external idlers, it can wrap any number of driven pulleys, limited only by the power capacity of the belt.
u73s1: This ability to bend the belt at the designer's whim allows it to take a complex or "serpentine" path.
u74s1: The entire belt may be tensioned by a single idler pulley.
u75s1: The nomenclature used for belt sizes varies by region and trade.
u76s1: An automotive belt with the number "740K6" or "6K740" indicates a belt 74 inches (190 cm) in length, 6 ribs wide, with a rib pitch of 9⁄64 of an inch (3.6 mm) (a standard thickness for a K series automotive belt would be 4.5mm).
u77s1: A metric equivalent would be usually indicated by "6PK1880" whereby 6 refers to the number of ribs, PK refers to the metric PK thickness and pitch standard, and 1880 is the length of the belt in millimeters.
u78s1: === Ribbed belt === A ribbed belt is a power transmission belt featuring lengthwise grooves.
u79s1: It operates from contact between the ribs of the belt and the grooves in the pulley.
u80s1: Its single-piece structure is reported to offer an even distribution of tension across the width of the pulley where the belt is in contact, a power range up to 600 kW, a high speed ratio, serpentine drives (possibility to drive off the back of the belt), long life, stability and homogeneity of the drive tension, and reduced vibration.
u81s1: The ribbed belt may be fitted on various applications: compressors, fitness bikes, agricultural machinery, food mixers, washing machines, lawn mowers, etc.
u82s1: === Film belts === Though often grouped with flat belts, they are actually a different kind.
u83s1: They consist of a very thin belt (0.5–15 millimeters or 100–4000 micrometres) strip of plastic and occasionally rubber.
u84s1: === Timing belts === Timing belts (also known as toothed, notch, cog, or synchronous belts) are a positive transfer belt and can track relative movement.
u85s1: These belts have teeth that fit into a matching toothed pulley.
u86s1: Camshafts of automobiles, miniature timing systems, and stepper motors often utilize these belts.
u87s1: Timing belts need the least tension of all belts and are among the most efficient.
u88s1: Timing belts with a helical offset tooth design are available.
u89s1: The chevron pattern design is self-aligning and does not make the noise that some timing belts make at certain speeds, and is more efficient at transferring power (up to 98%).
u90s1: The advantages of timing belts include clean operation, energy efficiency, low maintenance, low noise, non slip performance, versatile load and speed capabilities.
u91s1: Disadvantages include a relatively high purchase cost, the need for specially fabricated toothed pulleys, less protection from overloading, jamming, and vibration due to their continuous tension cords, the lack of clutch action (only possible with friction-drive belts), and the fixed lengths, which do not allow length adjustment (unlike link V-belts or chains).
u92s1: === Specialty belts === Belts normally transmit power on the tension side of the loop.
u93s1: However, designs for continuously variable transmissions exist that use belts that are a series of solid metal blocks, linked together as in a chain, transmitting power on the compression side of the loop.
u94s1: == Standards for use == The open belt drive has parallel shafts rotating in the same direction, whereas the cross-belt drive also bears parallel shafts but rotate in opposite direction.
u95s1: The former is far more common, and the latter not appropriate for timing and standard V-belts unless there is a twist between each pulley so that the pulleys only contact the same belt surface.
u96s1: Nonparallel shafts can be connected if the belt's center line is aligned with the center plane of the pulley.
u97s1: Industrial belts are usually reinforced rubber but sometimes leather types.
u98s1: Non-leather, non-reinforced belts can only be used in light applications.
u99s1: It is midway through the surfaces in film and flat belts and dependent on cross-sectional shape and size in timing and V-belts.
u100s1: Actual pulley speeds tend to be 0.5–1% less than generally calculated because of belt slip and stretch.
u101s1: In timing belts, the inverse ratio teeth of the belt contributes to the exact measurement.
u102s1: The speed of the belt is: === International use standards === Standards include: ISO 9563:
u103s1: This standard specifies requirements and test methods for endless power transmission V-belts and V-ribbed belts. ISO 4184:
u104s1: This standard specifies the dimensions of classical and narrow V-belts for general use.
u105s1: ISO 9981: This standard deals with the dimensions of rubber synchronous belt drives.
u106s1: This standard covers the dimensions of polyurethane synchronous belt drives. DIN 22101:
u107s1: This standard covers the design principles for belt conveyors used in bulk material handling, including safety requirements and testing methods.
u108s1: This standard specifies the dimensions, tolerances, and quality requirements for roller chain drives, which include belts and sprockets.
u109s1: ANSI/RMA IP-20 is a standard developed by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the Rubber Manufacturers Association (RMA) that focuses on elastomeric belts used in industrial applications.
u110s1: This standard covers important aspects such as dimensions and tolerances, ensuring that the belts perform reliably and efficiently in various industrial settings.
u111s1: SAE J1459 is a standard developed by the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) that focuses on automotive V-belts and V-ribbed belts.
u112s1: These belts are used in various automotive applications, such as power transmission between the engine and different accessories, including the alternator, power steering pump, air conditioning compressor, and water pump.
u113s1: The standard specifies test procedures, performance requirements, and dimensions to ensure the belts are reliable, durable, and suitable for automotive use.
u114s1: ASTM D378 is a standard developed by the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), which focuses on the testing of conveyor belts used in various industries for specific applications.
u115s1: Conveyor belts are essential for material handling and transportation in industries such as mining, construction, agriculture, and manufacturing.
u116s1: ASTM D378 covers the testing methods to evaluate conveyor belts for performance characteristics, such as fire resistance and oil resistance, ensuring that they meet safety and operational requirements.
u117s1: type of drive unit (electric motor, internal combustion engine); service environment (oily, wet, dusty); driven unit loads (jerky, shock, reversed); and pulley-belt arrangement (open, crossed, turned).
u118s1: When corrected, the power is compared to rated powers of the standard belt cross-sections at particular belt speeds to find a number of arrays that perform best.
u119s1: It is generally either large diameters or large cross-section that are chosen, since, as stated earlier, larger belts transmit this same power at low belt speeds as smaller belts do at high speeds.
u120s1: Minimum pulley diameters are limited by the elongation of the belt's outer fibers as the belt wraps around the pulleys.
u121s1: Small pulleys increase this elongation, greatly reducing belt life.
u122s1: Minimal pulley diameters are often listed with each cross-section and speed, or listed separately by belt cross-section.
u123s1: After the cheapest diameters and belt section are chosen, the belt length is computed.
u124s1: If endless belts are used, the desired shaft spacing may need adjusting to accommodate standard-length belts.
u125s1: It is often more economical to use two or more juxtaposed V-belts, rather than one larger belt.
u126s1: In large speed ratios or small central distances, the angle of contact between the belt and pulley may be less than 180°.
u127s1: Smaller contact angles mean less area for the belt to obtain traction, and thus the belt carries less power.
u128s1: === Belt friction === Belt drives depend on friction to operate, but excessive friction wastes energy and rapidly wears the belt.
u129s1: Factors that affect belt friction include belt tension, contact angle, and the materials used to make the belt and pulleys.
u130s1: === Belt tension === Power transmission is a function of belt tension.
u131s1: However, also increasing with tension is stress (load) on the belt and bearings.
u132s1: The ideal belt is that of the lowest tension that does not slip in high loads.
u133s1: Belt tensions should also be adjusted to belt type, size, speed, and pulley diameters.
u134s1: Belt tension is determined by measuring the force to deflect the belt a given distance per inch (or mm) of pulley.
u135s1: Timing belts need only adequate tension to keep the belt in contact with the pulley.
u136s1: === Belt wear === Fatigue, more so than abrasion, is the culprit for most belt problems.
u137s1: High belt tension; excessive slippage; adverse environmental conditions; and belt overloads caused by shock, vibration, or belt slapping all contribute to belt fatigue.
u138s1: === Belt vibration === Vibration signatures are widely used for studying belt drive malfunctions.
u139s1: Some of the common malfunctions or faults include the effects of belt tension, speed, sheave eccentricity and misalignment conditions.
u140s1: The effect of sheave Eccentricity on vibration signatures of the belt drive is quite significant.
u141s1: When the top section of a belt is in resonance, the vibrations of the machine is increased.
u142s1: However, an increase in the machine vibration is not significant when only the bottom section of the belt is in resonance.
u143s1: The vibration spectrum has the tendency to move to higher frequencies as the tension force of the belt is increased.
u144s1: Belt replacement is an obvious solution, and eventually the mandatory one (because no belt lasts forever).
u145s1: Often, though, before the replacement option is executed, retensioning (via pulley centerline adjustment) or dressing (with any of various coatings) may be successful to extend the belt's lifespan and postpone replacement.
u146s1: Belt dressings are typically liquids that are poured, brushed, dripped, or sprayed onto the belt surface and allowed to spread around; they are meant to recondition the belt's driving surfaces and increase friction between the belt and the pulleys.
u147s1: Some belt dressings are dark and sticky, resembling tar or syrup; some are thin and clear, resembling mineral spirits.
u148s1: === Specifications === To fully specify a belt, the material, length, and cross-section size and shape are required.
u149s1: Timing belts, in addition, require that the size of the teeth be given.
u150s1: The length of the belt is the sum of the central length of the system on both sides, half the circumference of both pulleys, and the square of the sum (if crossed) or the difference (if open) of the radii.
u151s1: When adding to the length of either side, the length of the belt increases, in a similar manner to the Pythagorean theorem.
u152s1: On the other hand, in a crossed belt drive the sum rather than the difference of radii is the basis for computation for length.
u153s1: So the wider the small drive increases, the belt length is higher.
